utterances.text: Can you please first explain to me what this really is, because this is the first time I see it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please go to the last page of the B/C/S version. At the bottom of the page, it says: "M., Mirza."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the document articulated in this way, this could have been written by anyone in Prijedor or in the wider region. I must point out that minutes of the municipal board of the SDA never looked like this document. We can just have a look. The date is stated the 24th of October, 1991. And only a couple of names are given, and then again, the 30th of October, 1991. No signature, no recording clerk, no stamp. My signature is not there. No agenda, no attendance. Things that are normally kept and recorded at our meetings. And then several lines later, a different date, the 13th of September, 1991, and then the 20th of November, 1991, out of nowhere. These were not SDA meetings, and I have no idea what this document really is. As I have been well informed by persons who were subjected to most terrible interrogations, false accusations, false documents by the -- implanted by the intelligence service, I really don't think that it document belonged to anyone who was a member of the SDA. I would say that this document had nothing to do with anything like that, and it was certainly -- it is certainly not a document of the municipal board of the SDA. I think it's obvious. If you just have a look at the document, you see immediately that it has nothing to do with the municipal board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would the witness be so kind and read out from -- in B/C/S the fourth -- the four-last lines on the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The 12th of May, 1992, meeting in Hambarine for the eventuality that the local commune cannot meet. The decision is reached by Refik, crossed out, Sefik Krkic and C. Pezo, M. Mirza." So the names of Camil Pezo, Sefik Krkic, and M. Mirza were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that Mr. Kenjar and Mr. Bahonjic were in charge of obtaining weapons for Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Sead Sivac was in charge of obtaining weapons for Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact Mr. Tadic was in charge of obtaining weapons for Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that gentlemen Kadiric, Hopovac, and Sikiric, were in charge of obtaining weapons for the Brdo area and Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Rufad Suljanovic was in charge of obtaining weapons for Puharska?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Are you stating that they were, and do you have any proof of that? Because your question was not a question; it was a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just to interrupt, could -- to be on the safe side, could the witness be himself read out the first two lines of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is quite illegible. I would prefer to stick to the English translation, if you agree. I will give it my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would caution -- inform the Court, as far as I know, I don't believe this is an official translation. I could be wrong, but I think they are only official if there is an ERN number attached to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As you may know, there is some knowledge of the language on the Bench as well. Therefore, in case of doubt, we would ask kindly that you try to read at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. "For weapons" -- this next word I really can't make out. Then the next word is "SDA." And then probably "in charge. Kozarac, Kenya Bahonjic; Trnopolje, Sead Sivac; Kozarusa, Tadic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop here. We can already identify a certain discrepancy between that what we heard and can read in the transcript, and that we can read in the English version. So therefore, it's better when we come back to this document to start with the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Mujadzic is not aware of the document --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is sure is that a document of this kind cannot be a document emanating from the SDA. Normally, in cases of official meetings of the SDA, one would have the indication whether the board in question was a local one or a municipal one. There would have been other indications pointing to the authenticity of the document. This is simply a record made by someone. It could be just about anyone's note coming from the person who was also perhaps ill-intentioned. You could have written a document of this kind yourself. Is there anything in this document that tells us about the fact that it can be linked to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Camil Pezo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the SDA Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the SDA Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the SDA Crisis Staff that you mentioned yesterday, this Crisis Staff, the SDA Crisis Staff, had nothing to do with any state competence as it was established after a number of events which led to the establishment of such a body. The SDA Crisis Staff was set up after Radovan Karadzic's threats and after the intentions of the general staff to carry out a putsch became manifest. This was the intention of several officers within the leadership of the military. And also, there was an idea promoted by several JNA officers that leaders of the SDA should be arrested and their property confiscated. That was the reason for the establishment of this body. Its objective was to guarantee the safety of the party and its members. This staff can by no means be linked to the Crisis Staff whose president was Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this Crisis Staff was established on the 23rd of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it took place much later, but I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You stated in your testimony on Tuesday, page 46, line 12 of Tuesday's transcript the following: "The only possibility that I saw at the time was to evacuate the population from the occupied area to the territory of western Krajina which, at the time, was under the control of the BH Territorial Defence which would later become the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Bench would like to follow. You said 46, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: An extract, as I've already said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I extracted it, I tried to avoid this, as I've already said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "The only possibility I could see" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can read it in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 40 [as interpreted], line 12: [In English] "The only possibility I could see was to evacuate the population from the occupied area to the area of the western Krajina, then controlled by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was later to become the BH army." [Interpretation] Is this true, Dr. Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So at the time, there was a territory which was controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was called at the time the Territorial Defence? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, do not misinterpret my statement. Would you please read the text as it is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a territory at the time which was controlled by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 46, line 22 of the same transcript, you spoke about the period of time which followed the takeover. I will read it in English. [In English] "That's why I allowed a negotiating team to be set up, although I took no part in this myself because I thought it was pointless." [Interpretation] You said that you had allowed for this negotiating team to be set up.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I have to ask you to read the exact words of my testimony once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] "That's why I allowed the negotiating team to be set up, although I took no part in this myself because I thought it was pointless." [Interpretation] Did they address you with the permission to do this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the word "allow" in the English language can be translated differently. I think that I originally said in B/C/S that I permitted, and not allowed. These two words have different meanings in my language. In the English language, they can be synonyms. But let me explain the context of my statement at the time. It is true that there was a group of people who believed that an agreement could be reached through negotiations with the newly established Serbian municipality and the SDS Crisis Staff. But I indicated that the group of people who thought that this was unreasonable and senseless was more numerous. So if we should follow a democratic procedure, then my opinion was a majority one. Had the decision been made to this effect, then there would have been no negotiations. Then it would have been decided that there would be no negotiations. However, my influence could be felt all the same because I permitted this minority to negotiate in order not to miss even the slightest opportunity, slightest possibility, to avoid the conflict. This is what I had in mind when I testified about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I simply wanted to ask you whether you had any say in the setting up of this negotiating team.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, the majority was against, but that I made sure that those people who were in favour of negotiations were allowed to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you had sent your family to Croatia. I think the date in question was the 13th of April, 1992. Were you the only person who had any inkling about the upcoming events, or were there other people who removed their families from Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, a large number of buses were leaving with the Prijedor residents who were leaving the town because they knew what was going to happen. As I said, there were local bus lines who carried people out of Prijedor. So obviously, I was not the one only who had done that. There were many similar cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Something is missing from the interpretation. You said that even some extraordinary bus lines had been introduced. This is not in the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that anyone had introduced such extraordinary bus lines. I simply said that due to the overall demand, private bus owners, private -- small, private transport companies on their own had introduced such extraordinary bus lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary to have a break now. But before we do this, we have still before us four sheets of paper tendered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Your Honours' criteria for the admission of documents does not relate to authenticity. It is not a criteria. However, I would just like to point out on this document the 20th November, 1991 entry, written with the UN and The Hague, and just point out that this is several years before the establishment of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It has been stated earlier by the parties that, and, of course, the Bench is aware, that numerous documents are on the market which may be not correct, may be correct, and, of course, it's for the evaluation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- It's for the evaluation of evidence later on to decide on the contents of the authenticity. No doubt, the witness already pointed out some perspectives. But please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness offered us the explanation, and I see also that this document is not reliable, does not carry out reliability, so the Defence would not offer this document into evidence. We would not. Because I can't see how we would be able to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will decide after the break on this point. Thank you. We resume at 12.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we proceed, I have to announce a decision of the Bench, that the document that was provisionally marked as D9 will be admitted into evidence as Document J3. The reason for this is, of course, that we have to know what is explained by the witness in the transcript, and in case we need it later on for the proof, if any, that there might be documents on the market that might be not correct, to put it this way. We have to go probably into details, but first of all, the purpose is that we can find out what was the witness' statement and what was the basis therefore. Then the cross-examination may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Mujadzic, do you know where Dr. Stakic comes from, from which town?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, he comes from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there a large partisan cemetery in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the 1st Krajina Proletarian Brigade was established in Omarska and had residents of Omarska and neighbouring villages as its members?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the name of Milomir Stakic's grandfather, Milos Stakic, is carved in stone together with the names of other partisans at the monument at Mrakovica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Military units in Travnik and Bihac, did they also have medical corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of this medical corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your parents spent some time in Trnopolje. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they eventually leave Trnopolje; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when they left Trnopolje, but they did at one point in time. If necessary, in private session, I can explain the circumstances of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many weapons were surrendered to the army after the army and the Territorial Defence clash in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any of the people from Hambarine go to the Kurevo woods with weapons? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about it, although I never found out the exact number of these people, nor their precise location, nor how they were grouped. I only mentioned in my testimony that we tried to get in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked in Bihac after you left the Prijedor area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a camp for Serbs in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any refugees from Bihac in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you currently cooperating with the information and documentation agency of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you before cooperate with the Yugoslavia state security?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hereby conclude my examination of the witness. Mr. Mujadzic, I thank you for your effort in answering our questions. Your Honours, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Very brief. I want to leave time for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Witness, in the document D7 -- I don't know if you have that before you, D7 -- there is a reference in that document to civil disobedience. I think you can answer this question without the document at this point. Was there any talk among any members of the SDA of a campaign of civil disobedience in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the original idea of Muhamed Cehajic, and there were other people who advocated this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cehajic use a term to describe that besides the words "civil disobedience"? Did he use a term to describe that campaign?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said a Ghandi-like resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this is worth the time. I wanted to point out several quotes from D7, but if the item itself is in the record, I could do that when the witness is not present, or just point out to Your Honours in our final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Otherwise, you would leave the question for us. So please feel free.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to D7, do you have that now before you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the very first page, under the 30th of April, after the quote by Beco, meaning Becir Medunjanin, there is a proposal: "Since we have a lot of people without weapons, men should leave the weapons, as they leave the shift." Can you explain that? If that makes sense to you, from what you know about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please just remind me where is this exactly on the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the first page, at the top, the second item is "proposal." Do you have D7? It should have the number --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, that's correct. This speaks for itself, speaks about the facts at that time in Kozarac and Prijedor. There were not enough weapons for everyone, for all men of military age. There was only an insufficient number of weapons, so people left their own weapons after leaving the shift so these weapons could be used by others who take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll now just refer to a few other portions of this document and ask you after I've finished all of those references to comment. On the same page, attributed to Kemal Fazlic, it states "Is there a plan? No. Kozarac will not defended by arms. Therefore, everything should be undertaken before opening fire. Wisdom is needed." About four or five lines down is the number 1, "the issue of the ultimatum for surrendering weapons. No surrender. We shall only respond if attacked." On the next page, page 2, about the bottom one third of that page, on the upper right, it's page 326, it's handwritten, attributed to Kenjar S., "civil disobedience should also be discussed with the other areas. In Kozarac, some guys are provoking too much." On page 325, the second quote, attributed Suljo: "If Kozarusa does not receive help it will surrender at all the checkpoints." And then on page 320, with the date on the top, 6 June, 1992, under miscellaneous, there's a statement attributed to (redacted). "We have established the peace headquarters consisting of" -- and it appears to be either whited out or illegible for some reason -- "members taken from all parties operating in the area. We have published a declaration and a written statement which has been broadcast on the radio. Copies of both the declaration and the statement have been submitted to Hamdija Kahrimanovic. A team with a mixed membership has been all current problems ranging from shooting incidents to economic issues. Duties and patrols have been introduced. Mixed patrols for the protection of all citizens in the Kozarusa local Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commune have been established. There should not be any conflict among us until the status of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been resolved." On page 318, in the middle of the page, attributed to Velic: "We are doing everything we can to preserve the peace, but it seems we are not going to succeed." And I believe the next quote I was going to have was on page 315, Bahonjic, but you have already read that to us. On page 313, there's a statement attributed to Pasic, the second speaker, and the last two lines are: "I propose we are not in favour of war, but we are unable to set up a municipality. I do not believe that weapons should be given up, nor will I sign a statement of loyalty." Doctor, are these quotes, that I've just given, consistent with your recollection of the position of various members of the SDA prior to the outbreak of a full conflict and the attack on Kozarac on the 24th of May?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I tried to say, in as many words. There were a number of different opinions, but all these opinions could be roughly divided into two camps. Those who believed that something could be achieved by negotiating with the aggressor, and those who believed that whatever was done, there would have been a predetermined scenario in response to it, and that the Serbian army, that is, the SDS, would continue as planned. It is clear from these testimonies that you have now read, it really was like that. Both sides, regardless of everything, made enormous efforts to preserve peace and to avoid conflicts, as best as they could. Because everyone knew that they didn't really stand a chance of resisting such a modern and well-equipped and well-armed army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In private session, you told us about something that happened at Trnopolje with your parents. How did your parents get to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I say? There was a general order -- I'm not sure whether it was an order, but the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor evacuated all the population and transferred most of the population to the Trnopolje camp, and then from that camp, people were selected, so to speak. People who were on their lists, on their wanted lists, and many other people who were on no lists. They just happened by a guard's arrogance or by the arrogant behaviour of people who served as guards in the camp. So these people were selected randomly sent to the camps and killed in the Omarska camp, which was much worse than the Trnopolje camp. Many girls were raped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Just in the interests of time, I'm trying to keep it short. What happened to the home that your parents were living in, your family home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theirs was the first house in Prijedor. On the 23rd of May when the tanks set out for Hambarine, the first house to be shelled, the first house that was burned and destroyed. Although there was no reason for that. The whole town was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During your testimony, you mentioned two names, Dr. Zeljko Sikora, and Dr. Sadikovic. Could you please tell us the fate of both persons.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both killed in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know this for sure, or are they still missing persons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Sadikovic, the body that was identified as the body of Dr. Sadikovic, was dug up recently in the Sanski Most area. As for Dr. Sikora, several other witnesses from the Omarska camp stated, confirmed, that they saw him killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned your relation to Dr. Zeljko Sikora, but not the one to Dr. Sadikovic. Could you please explain what was the role of Dr. Sadikovic, what was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Sadikovic was a very well-trained, educated physician. He worked in Africa as a UN physician. He came from a well-respected local family from Prijedor. We were close friends. And we knew each other quite well. Dr. Sadikovic assumed a fully neutral position. His wife was Serbian. And he never, in any sense, joined the SDA, or never had any political commitment at all, in any party. He made enormous efforts to preserve peace in Prijedor. Have I answered your question, Your Honours? Perhaps there was something I haven't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. As you mentioned a number of issues exhaustively, I have to jump from one issue to the other, unfortunately. The next would be, was the police station part of the centre for state security in Banja Luka or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was part of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you quite sure? Because in an unofficial, of course, summary, it is said that the police station was not a part of the centre for state security in Banja Luka, as Prijedor did not join the Serb Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this needs clarification. Officially, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina is organised, is based -- divided into the central Ministry in Sarajevo which had regional security services centres in Banja Luka, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Mostar, Zenica, Doboj, in several different areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Each of these regional centres had under its authority public security stations. The establishment of the Autonomous Region of Krajina following the establishment, the leaders of the regional centre of Banja Luka security services separated itself from the legal framework of the Bosnia and Herzegovina ministry. As the minister sent many of his decisions to public security stations, thereby bypassing the regional centres whose role was more to coordinate. The Prijedor police station wanted to continue to maintain its links with the legal ministry in Sarajevo. Our proposal was, in order to overcome the situation, as the newly established police centre in the Autonomous Region of Krajina demanded that all communications with Sarajevo be stopped, and that the only orders to be obeyed were those coming from the police of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So the proposal was to continue subordination to Sarajevo, but that a degree of coordination was to be established also with the police of the Krajina region so that clashes may be avoided. But apart from that, the police of the Autonomous Region of Krajina denied its own legality by separating from the central Ministry, The Sarajevo Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not sure how successful I've been in explaining the nature of these relationships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to thank you for this clarification. Could you please, if you know, tell us who was superior to the commanders responsible in Omarska or Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean direct superior authority? To the best of my knowledge, the commander of the Omarska camp was Milan Kovacevic, also known as Mico. And the commander of the Trnopolje camp was Slobodan Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They had to obey the orders of which persons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took orders from the Crisis Staff. As I have already testified in a number of documents, for example, the order, the prohibition to release prisoners from the Omarska camp, bearing the signature of the Crisis Staff, where it is obvious that the Crisis Staff is behind this decision, and it also enclaves the relationship of subordination of the Omarska camp staff, command staff, to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Crisis Staff on which level?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, it was the Crisis Staff at the level of Prijedor municipality, but some of the decisions came from the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What role, if any, played the police in the camps, the municipal police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think back, Your Honours, there was a document presented -- there was an order to the police to set up the camp in Omarska, and there are several other orders than I cannot recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm aware of this, but please understand, we can't rely only, as I pointed out vis-a-vis the Defence already, we can't rely on statute only or order. The question is whether or not these orders were executed and what do you know yourself about the facts?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in practice, Simo Drljaca's police were more than obedient as concerns their orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I withdraw the question with your answer would be only based on hearsay. Can you tell us something about the takeover of the television transmitter on Kozara mountain?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, the transmitter was taken over by the JNA. Some of our people went there to see what was happening, and they saw that the transmitter was guarded by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The person of Dr. Stakic, what was your impression? You were quoted as saying that Dr. Stakic was a quiet person, but had hard-line beliefs. Can you explain this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My familiarity with Dr. Stakic from the prewar period and my impression of him as a man who was in no way different from everyone else. So as far as his character is concerned, he was a stable person, a quiet person. However, later on, in my conversations with him, after the Serbian municipality was founded or when the reserve military came back from Croatia and carried out acts of provocation in Prijedor, the whole sequence of events, I tried to talk to him on several occasions. I appealed to our friendship, to our sense of companionship, because we were both physicians. It was then that I understood from our conversations two different things: Firstly, that Stakic was firmly convinced that whatever he did, whatever he did, he did out of conviction, because he really believed in it. And his convictions were those of the Karadzic hardliners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you compare the roles of Mr. Miskovic and Dr. Stakic, as regards their influence in the so-called takeover in Prijedor, whom do you regard as more influential?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I believe that Mr. Miskovic, at the time of the takeover, was the most influential person in the SDS. However, I find it very interesting that Mr. Miskovic later does not appear as a member of the Crisis Staff. At that time, it surprised me because, judging by his convictions and the influence he exerted, he appeared likely to be a member of that body and be in it, rather than behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is your actual role in politics, if any, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The question is today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the end of the war, that is, since the Dayton accords, as I completed my mandate as a deputy, I finished my political commitment and my political involvement. I never considered myself as a politician. My only reason for getting involved in these, let us call them political events, although they were much more than that, was to contribute to democratic changes taking place in the former Yugoslavia. But the later course of events led to all the things that you're also familiar with. So transported on a wave of these events, I stayed in politics until 1996, until the end of the war. As soon as the war ended, I went back to my daily job and was no longer involved in politics. Currently, I am (redacted)and have nothing to do with any of the political structures in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The residence may be redacted from the transcript, please. Thank you. Judge Fassi Fihri, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you finished the examination-in-chief on Tuesday, the 28th of May, by saying that Dr. Stakic was promoting hatred between the communities and was undermining any feeling of tolerance between the communities. Could you tell us what are the elements that allow you to be so affirmative in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if possible, could you refer me to this portion in my testimony. I don't remember having stated something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the transcript, last page, if you want I can read out exactly what you said. "That's why Karadzic fully trusted Dr. Stakic, because Dr. Stakic comes from an area that is dominated by the Chetnik. He tried to introduce a gap between the Serbians and the Bosnians, and he tried to undermine the feeling of tolerance and the conviction that it was possible for these two communities to live together in the area. By killing so many people, he wanted to promote hatred amongst the population that could only be an obstacle to the possibility for these communities in the area to live together."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement indicates that Stakic was a trusted person, a trusted man by Karadzic. The proof of that can be found in the fact that he was elected as member of the Executive Board and was part of the leadership of the SDS, also the fact that he was appointed to the Crisis Staff as its member, which could not be done without the approval of the centre, which all means that Dr. Karadzic trusted Stakic. That concerns the first part of my statement. But the second part concerns Dr. Karadzic. I was talking about Dr. Karadzic when I said that "he was trying to create a rift between the two communities" which had, in the past, been tolerant of each other by having this large number of people killed, and it is true that a large number of people were killed in Prijedor. This tolerance, this traditional tolerance has, therefore, been undermined in the area of Prijedor. I never said that Dr. Stakic personally incited hatred and attempted to undermine tolerance in the area. I just refer to him as a trusted person by Dr. Karadzic, and I believe that I explained this to the Chamber. But that the idea of the destruction of this local and traditional tolerance came from Dr. Karadzic. And I also explained how he implemented this plan, this idea, by killing several thousands of people in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FASSI FIHRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, in your testimony on Monday, pages 15 and 55 of the transcript, you mentioned Serbian Radical Party established in Prijedor, which in 1990 entered an election coalition with the Serbian Democratic Party and stated that Mr. Stakic was also involved in setting up of the Serbian Radical Party. In this respect, can you tell us in more detail, what was the Serbian Radical Party and its programme?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian Radical Party is a royalist party in its nature and programme. They based their ideas on some basic principles of the royalistic movement which was led during the Second World War by Draza Mihajlovic and his military, that is, the Chetniks and their formations. These Chetnik formations during the First World War, not the second one but the First World War, did indeed play a major role in defending the kingdom of Serbia at the time. And in that respect, one can argue that they played a very positive role. However, during the Second World War, these units perpetrated atrocious crimes against non-Serb population in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And not only Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also Serbia and Montenegro. Let me mention, for instance, the crime which was committed in Foca, when, in one single day, 7.000 Bosniaks were killed. So by establishing this kind of party in Omarska, the party with this kind of tradition and this kind of background, the Bosniak population became mistrustful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was the position and role of Dr. Stakic in the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have much information on that really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On what condition the Serbian Radical Party entered the coalition with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Vracar who, according to what I know was the president of the Serbian Radical Party, was in a preelection coalition with the Serbian Democratic Party. He was given a position of the candidate, a joint candidate, of the SDS and the Serbian Radical Party. He was nominated as a deputy to the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some other members of the Serbian Radical Party were also on the same list with the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian Democratic Alliance for the municipal level of elections. So it was a classical type of a party coalition. Later on, after the first government was installed, after the election, and this is something that I'm not quite sure about, I do not have any reliable information on that, and it is perhaps worth exploring, but I think that Dr. Stakic became the vice-president of the municipality on behalf of this coalition, the coalition of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian Radical Party, as a representative of the Serbian Radical Party. Once again, I am emphasising the fact that this is something that I'm not sure about. I'm basing this on something that I heard from other people, but I am sure that this can be checked if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. In your testimony, you also mentioned the Patriotic League, headed by Mr. Halilovic. Can you tell us, what was the Patriotic League? Was it a party or some other entity?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Patriotic League is an organisation of patriots of Bosnia and Herzegovina who share the same idea, that is, the defence of their homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Having had the experience of Slovenia, which thanks to a very high level of organisation and preparedness, managed to oppose the JNA and repel its aggression, a segment of population, comprising some free-thinking citizens and some former JNA officers, thought that it would be very useful and good to establish an organisation such as the Patriotic League. Its coat of arms was the traditional coat of arms of the Kotramanic Dynasty. This coat of arms had a blue background and golden fleur-de-lys, which is an influence of the Anjou dynasty, and traditional relations between this dynasty and the Anjou dynasty. In France, it tells of a long-standing history of relationship between my country and that part of Europe. And this Patriotic League gathered, as I said, a large number of patriots or the people who considered Bosnia and Herzegovina to be their homeland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you know the first name of Mr. Halilovic, and did Mr. Halilovic ever hold any position in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know his name. Sefer, Sefer Halilovic. He was later appointed by the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the commander of the main staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: In your testimony on Tuesday, transcript page 52, you stated that on the 16th of May, a public communique was made to the effect that the former JNA, in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was no longer Yugoslav People's Army but was being renamed into the Serbian army. Did the Serbian army become the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia and Croatia, the majority of the JNA personnel were stationed in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A significant number of officers from Serbia, officers who, by virtue of their birth did not belong to Bosnia and Herzegovina, found themselves in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, this was both de facto and de jure Yugoslav People's Army. Later on, this organisation proclaimed itself Serbian army, together with the local forces and the reservists from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, members of the Serb population, the Serbian community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Who became the commander in chief of that army and to whom he was subordinated and reported to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first commander of the Serbian army -- I'm sorry, I cannot remember who the first commander of the Serbian army was. There have been several of them after it was declared the Serbian army. So I cannot remember the first one. I know that he was responsible to the president of the Serbian republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between the Serbian army and the Crisis Staff of ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To illustrate this relationship, I should like to give you an example of what I was able to hear on a tape which, at one point in time, was given to us deputies, to the parliament. It was actually given to me by the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The tape was the recording of a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and the command of what was then still the JNA at the time of the aggression against Croatia. It was a lengthy conversation, but let me briefly tell you about its contents. The Serb population apparently did not respond to the mobilisation which was ordered by JNA at the time in large enough numbers. There had even been several incidents which were likely to lead to an overall rebellion amongst the organised conscripts. I believe it was Colonel Kostic who then called Karadzic and asked him to intervene urgently and to use his political influence to calm people down and to convince them to accept the mobilisation into the JNA. In subsequent contacts after the JNA, which was situated and located in Bosnia and Herzegovina, declared itself to be the Serbian army, they placed themselves under the command of the then proclaimed president of the Serbian republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. As for the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the commander of the Serbian army, now, I don't know whether you're referring only to the corps of the Banja Luka region, to the command of the Banja Luka corps or...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On the republican level and the municipal level, let us say.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the republican level, it was Radovan Karadzic who was de facto the civilian commander of the army of the Serbian republic. As for the local level, no doubt there was close cooperation between the two. However, since the hierarchy within the military is a direct one in terms of operations and specific military actions, such orders and instructions always came from the main staff of the army and from the leadership of Republika Srpska; whereas at the local level, this cooperation was somewhat different. Local politicians were able to have influence over the military who were stationed in their area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other questions from the side of the parties emanating only from the responses of the witness to the questions put forward by the Judges? I can see no other questions. Then it remains only for me to thank you very much for your patience and for all your information given through the last four days. The trial stays adjourned until Tuesday, 3.00 in the afternoon.
